source.title: How Do LLMs Encode Scientific Quality? An Empirical Study Using Monosemantic Features from Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Michael McCoubrey; Angelo Salatino; Francesco Osborne; Enrico Motta

record.tranche_reason: Uses SAE-derived monosemantic features as an analysis tool for predicting bibliometric proxies for research quality; it does not test whether neuron poles have one main job or validate the fidelity or sufficiency of neuron explanations.
record.gate_note: The study extracts and qualitatively labels SAE features, then reports decision-tree accuracy for predicting citation, SJR, and h-index quartiles. Those are results about downstream prediction from the features, not measurements of the claim versions' neuron interpretability, feature-explanation fidelity, or neuron-based circuit sufficiency. They are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"]. The feature labels are qualitative descriptions, not a reported count or rate of interpretable features.
record.test_reason: The study uses Gemma Scope SAE features, not neurons, as inputs to decision trees that predict bibliometric quartiles (citations, SJR, h-index). It reports only prediction accuracy and qualitative feature labels. It never measures how many neurons or neuron poles have one job. It does not test explanation fidelity by inspection or by simulation, or neuron-based circuits. Since it does not rely on the neuron claim itself, T6 would also be defensible.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add two points: the decision trees beat the BERT baseline only on citation quartiles (0.6788 vs 0.6522 averaged), and BERT wins on SJR and h-index. Also, 9B-it at layer 20 did slightly best on average.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SAE activations averaged across tokens in generated paper summaries, then decision trees to predict bibliometric quartiles; it does not audit neuron poles or test explanation fidelity. The repository is a research-materials repo, not a replication of the neuron-pole audit.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports results for Gemma 2 2B at layer 20 and Gemma 2 9B-it at layers 20 and 31; it notes modestly higher performance for the 9B model at layer 20.

fits_no_version.finding: Among SAE features that decision trees selected, several received only ambiguous labels from the authors, e.g. 5 of 15 in Table 2 marked 'Has an ambiguous definition'. The authors call the academic-language features 'the least interpretable'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some decision-tree-selected Gemma Scope SAE features lack clear qualitative labels. This concerns SAE features chosen for prediction, not neurons.

record.problems: Feature descriptions are assigned qualitatively by researchers and may be subjective; the study uses only Gemma 2 models and bibliometric proxies. It does not validate the feature descriptions on held-out activating examples or measure the share of interpretable neuron poles.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the BERT comparator as a separate row because it is a text-classification baseline, not a measurement of the claim's object; its task accuracies are recorded as baselines. Omitted task and model averages in Table 1 because the per-task, per-configuration results are recorded separately.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or job-count shares.
No neuron interpretability shares across models or scales. Only Gemma 2 SAE features are used.
No comparison of architecture, regularization or tools for interpretable-neuron share.
No attribution graphs and no neuron-versus-replacement comparison.
Labels come from Neuronpedia inspection, but no test of whether they predict activations.

record.verdict_notes: All rows are correctly linked to none and set to cannot_determine. The BERT baseline is a comparator for a downstream task, not a control for the claim. The feature labels are SAE latents selected by a classifier, so they cannot yield an interpretable share for any version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B, count neuron poles by number of jobs, or quantify unexplained poles.
Does not measure shares of single-job neuron poles across models, architectures, or scales.
Does not study InceptionV1 examples, pose detection, or recursive generalization versus superposition.
Does not compare architecture, regularization, or tool effects on interpretability rates, or estimate interpretable shares for vision models.
Does not test whether neuron-based attribution graphs explain behavior or compare them with a replacement model.
Does not test explanations against held-out activating examples or measure whether they predict where neurons fire.
Does not simulate neuron explanations on new text or report the share attaining good automated scores.
